title: Michigan will not hire Trev Alberts as next AD: School could owe full buyout to ex-Texas A&M administrator - CBS Sports
description: Alberts was set to leave for his third job in three years, but is now thrown into flux
body:
Alberts was set to leave for his third job in three years, but is now thrown into flux
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                            
        
    Nov 24, 2026
                            
                    at
    2:04 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            4 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Trev Alberts has been informed that he will not be hired as the program's new athletic director by the search firm assisting with the hire. Alberts was set to leave Texas A&M for the new role. "The University of Michigan's search for its next athletic director is ongoing," a school spokesperson told CBS Sports' Brandon Marcello. "As we navigate a rapidly changing landscape in intercollegiate athletics, the values that define Michigan will guide our decisions and reinforce our commitment to excellence and integrity, both in the classroom and in competition."Alberts was expected to replace outgoing athletic director Warde Manuel. According to documents obtained by CBS Sports, an MOU was signed by Domenico Grasso (current Michigan president), C. Cybele Raver (incoming Michigan president) and Alberts on November 17th. It was not contingent on board of regents approval, nor a background check, according to a source familiar with the negotiation. Michigan is on the hook for a $4 million buyout from Texas A&M and $17.2 million under his current contract, bringing the final price tag to $21.2 million."Late last night, I was shocked and disheartened to learn that the University of Michigan had decided not to move forward with my appointment as its Director of Athletics despite having signed a binding Memorandum of Understanding," Alberts wrote in a statement. "I had already begun working on behalf of Michigan Athletics and was excited about the opportunities and challenges ahead."
"The egregious characterization of words taken out of context from a deposition regarding an incident that occurred years ago is wrong and unfair," Alberts continued. "I was informed that Michigan's general counsel had spoken with the general counsel of both Texas A&M and the University of Nebraska, as well as Nebraska's outside counsel, to inquire about the deposition. "I was further told that all three of those lawyers told Michigan's GC that I had done nothing wrong or inappropriate and had followed all applicable university policies and procedures. I am proud of my long track record of standing up for student-athletes and for following the rules and my core values. I wish the student-athletes, coaches and staff at the University of Michigan all the very best. My legal counsel and I are conferring on next steps."There was a previously scheduled meeting of the regents and Raver on Sunday, during which Raver gave no indication that Alberts' hire would not proceed. Regents were briefed on the details of the lawsuit.
"This was the president's decision; she made the decision [Monday] night," a Michigan university source told CBS Sports. "Board members expected the announcement of a hire Monday."CBS Sports' Brandon Marcello reached out to Texas A&M to inquire whether Alberts could return to his previous post. "Texas A&M announced earlier this week that Dr. John Thornton will serve as interim athletic director and will begin Dec. 1," a school spokesperson told Marcello. "The university remains on track and has engaged  a search firm to assist in identifying the next permanent athletic director."
The memorandum of understanding signed by multiple parties on Nov. 17 preceded FOIAball's reporting about Alberts' specific comments in a deposition, published Nov. 19, but the fact that Alberts was named in a civil Title IX lawsuit has been public since early 2024.During the deposition, Alberts was asked directly whether college coaches should ever have sex with athletes they are coaching. He answered that "it depends," especially with older pandemic-era players being closer in age to college coaches."It's simply optics regarding the deposition he gave in the Nebraska lawsuit, and the answer he gave in the deposition was completely accurate but taken out of context," a source familiar with the situation told CBS Sports.
As of Tuesday morning, Alberts has not received anything in writing beyond being contacted by the search firm (TurnkeyZRG) and being told that the process will not move forward. He has yet to hear directly from Michigan. It's currently unclear whether Alberts could return to his post at Texas A&M. The former Nebraska athletic director was set to take over a Michigan athletic department that has been embroiled in scandal over the past five years. The Wolverines fired football coach Sherrone Moore for cause after the 2025 season regarding an inappropriate relationship with a staff member. Michigan football was also the subject of multiple NCAA investigations and punishments under Jim Harbaugh. One of the first jobs for whoever Michigan lands on as athletics director will be evaluating the direction of the football program under embattled first-year coach Kyle Whittingham (the Wolverines are 6-5 headed into Saturday's rivalry game vs. Ohio State). 
Texas A&M announced Alberts' departure and named an interim athletic director on Monday. It's unclear whether Alberts could go back to College Station after publicly leaving. Texas A&M lost its last three athletic directors to other programs, including Alberts.

title: MLB CBA negotiations timeline: League, MLBPA trade new proposals over revenue sharing as Dec. 1 deadline nears - CBS Sports

body:
As the 2026 Major League Baseball offseason continues to unfold, something vitally important to the future of the sport quietly hums in the background: the ongoing negotiations over a new collective bargaining agreement. The collective bargaining agreement, or CBA  (or Basic Agreement, as it's known in a formal sense), is the negotiated accord between players and clubs -- i.e., the team owners and commissioner Rob Manfred, who represents their interests -- that governs the working relationship between the two parties, typically for a period of five years. It covers things as mundane as players' meal allowances and travel protocols and as vital as minimum salaries, the structure of free agency, revenue-sharing specifics, and roster sizes. Every CBA can be distilled down to a fight over money, or, more specifically, how the league's revenues will be divided between players and team owners. The first CBA covered the 1968 and 1969 seasons and was the first in professional sports history. That was the handiwork of Marvin Miller, the pioneering head of the Players Association (i.e., the players union) and belated Hall of Famer. It was Miller's organizing skills, foresight, and training as a union economist that allowed him to make the Players Association a viable and effective labor organization. Every CBA negotiation from 1972 through 1994-95 resulted in some form and scale of labor stoppage, whether a players' strike or an owner-implemented lockout. After the cancellation of the 1994 World Series because of the worst labor stoppage in the sport's history, a long run of peace followed. That peace lasted until the prior CBA negotiations, which resulted in a 99-day lockout forced by team owners and delayed the start of the 2022 season. 
        
            
                MLB's new CBA proposal would restrict free-agency contracts, raise minimum wage, but only with a salary cap
                
                    Dayn Perry                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
The current CBA negotiations have been underway for some time, and not surprisingly, the two sides remain far apart on several key issues. The biggest fight will be over the owners' renewed desire to implement a salary cap, which the union continues to view as a non-starter. The push for a cap has less to do with the notions of competitive balance and more to do with the ownership's internal belief that being the only non-salary-capped league among the major North American sports is harming franchise values. The cap, though, is but one of many pressing issues on which players and owners must find congruity.
Moving forward, the process will be uncertain and rife with posturing and pointed public comments from both sides. The hope, though, is that a new CBA will be agreed to before the middle of March 2027, at which point there's a high risk of having the 2027 season delayed or even abbreviated. To keep you informed of the twists and turns along the way to a new CBA, we've provided a detailed timeline of negotiations. That timeline will illuminate the important and finer points of the talks and, along the way, explain the implications of the various proposals coming from each side. The hope, of course, is that all of it culminates in a timely agreement that permits a fully intact and on-time 2027 season. Now let's begin. Nov. 24, 2026: MLB adjusts "salary escrow" proposal In earlier iterations of negotiations, MLB proposed a salary-escrow system like the ones found in the NBA and NHL. This would mean a percentage of player salaries is withheld in case league revenue projections fall short for a given year. If that's the case, then that money in escrow goes back to the league to cover the revenue shortfalls. If revenues are higher than projected, that excess is shared with the players. The MLBPA has pointedly opposed the escrow system on the grounds that it undermines the notion of guaranteed player salaries. In its latest statement on the negotiations, MLB withdrew the escrow proposal. "For months, union leadership has attacked the escrow provision used in other sports and mischaracterized the issue as the end of guaranteed contracts," MLB spokesperson Glen Caplin said in a statement. "MLB took another step today by withdrawing our escrow proposal, removing any doubt that every single guaranteed player contract will remain fully guaranteed in the new salary cap and floor system."
The specifics of the new proposal, which like all other league proposals thus far been tied to the players' accceptance of a cap and floor on team payrolls: No player compensation will be withheld in escrow. All existing contracts that contain a guarantee provision will remain fully guaranteed.Any new contract that contains a guarantee provision will be fully guaranteed. Note: any guarantee would still be subject to the guarantee provision contained in the player's contract (no change from the 2026 status quo).Any aggregate underpayment or overpayment to players in a given season will be incorporated into the calculation of the salary cap and floor in future seasons. In addition, following an overpayment, MLB would have the right to calculate the salary cap and floor using a revenue lag of up to two years.In response, interim union head Bruce Meyer released the following statement: "MLB today modified its salary cap proposal to 'eliminate' escrow, but once again it provides no real benefit under their proposed cap system. Instead of holding back player money each year, MLB's new proposal is to take that same amount of money out of players' pockets in the following year. It's a different way of achieving the same objective of the salary cap - to reduce and suppress player salaries and freedom of movement. This is yet another example of how MLB's salary cap proposal pits player against player, past, present, and future."Nov. 23, 2026: MLB and MLBPA make latest proposalsIn their latest bargaining session, the MLBPA maintained its previous proposals aimed to increase revenue sharing support for small market teams, including a mechanism designed to punish teams that do not put revenue sharing funds into the roster. The union also said the proposal is designed to remove "any league excuses for the continuation of blackouts."Here are the details of the union's latest proposal:Monetary rewards for revenue-sharing recipient clubs that qualify for the postseason ($20 million), fail to qualify but have a better record than the worst postseason qualifier ($20 million), or finish with a record above .500 ($10 million).Additional draft picks and international signing bonus pool space for revenue-sharing recipient clubs that sign their own free agents either as free agents, or one year prior to free agency.Similar draft and international signing incentives to revenue-sharing recipient clubs that sign players in free agency (regardless of prior club).Maintaining competitive balance picks in the amateur draft, and further lottery enhancements to deter tanking.Increased rewards for teams that promote top prospects to the big leagues rather than manipulate service time.As for MLB's proposal, it now includes a $1 million minimum salary (previous proposals were described as $1 million but not quite that amount), and a new series of bonuses for all player classes:Pre-arbitration players: $100,000 bonus for all pre-arbitration-eligible players who receive a full year of service time and spend less than half the season on the injured list.Arbitration-eligible players: Bonus equal to 5% of the player's base salary for those who avoid an arbitration hearing, including those who sign a multi-year contract that doesn't cover free agent years.Veteran players: Each team can award a $500,000 bonus to one player who has at least six years of service time and is signed to a one-year contract worth no more than $10 million.MLB's proposal is once again tied to the MLBPA's acceptance of a salary cap/floor system, which the players association has insisted it will never allow.
"The league's proposals today don't add a single dollar in overall player compensation as compared to prior proposals, and once again are expressly conditioned on accepting their salary cap and other anti-player restrictions," MLBPA executive director Bruce Meyer said in a statement. "Any supposed benefits to certain classes of players are simply taken out of the pockets of other players and are vastly outweighed by the negative effects of the cap and MLB's other restrictions. These negative effects include, but are not limited to, a drastic reduction in overall player compensation and benefits, the end of fully guaranteed contracts, and dramatic restrictions on players' career choices and freedom to contract."Nov. 20, 2026: Union proposes changes to international signing; MLB walks back exclusion of high school players from draftThe MLBPA on Friday put forth a series of proposed changes to the international signing structure. Notably, the union did not propose the implementation of an international draft, which the league has long sought. "We are committed to negotiating a system that preserves opportunities for future generations of players, protects young prospects from exploitation, and provides flexibility without further burdening international players with new artificial restrictions like a draft," MLBPA interim leader Bruce Meyer said in a statement released by the union. "Our proposals help build upon baseball's advances as an international game, while safeguarding the interests of young athletes who are the future of our sport."Specifically, the union's proposal calls for: 
Increasing team signing bonus pools used to sign international amateurs;Increasing the signing bonus pool exemption from $10,000 to $75,000 to improve bonuses at the lower end of the bonus range;Providing additional bonuses for players as they are promoted to higher levels;Establishing penalties for club conduct not permitted under the CBA. Eliminating pre-agreement arrangements by creating greater flexibility and less predictability within the system - strongly disincentivizing unlawful conduct by clubs;Allowing teams to more easily trade pool space and roll over any remaining pool space at the end of the signing period;Increasing the signing bonus pools of small-market teams by $1,000,000 during a single signing period within the 5-year agreement and by $500,000 for each signing period following a postseason appearance;Providing small market teams the ability to sign eligible players with limited foreign professional experience without affecting the signing of amateur players, by creating separate, independent signing bonus pools;Proving a financial reward for small-market teams reaching the postseason to be funded by the tax revenue collected from teams that exceed their signing bonus pool;Providing increased signing bonus pool space to small-market teams for having lost or having signed free agents or pending free agents.Also on Friday, MLB removed from the bargaining table an earlier proposal to exclude high school players from the annual MLB Draft. MLB spokesperson Glen Caplin said the following in a statement released by the league, which also includes a call for the implementation of an international draft: "In recognition of the feedback we received from the MLBPA on our domestic amateur proposal, we made a concession today by withdrawing our proposal on high school eligibility and proposed to maintain the current entry rules for domestic amateurs. On the international system, we continue to believe it is long past time to reform the system in ways that would address longstanding challenges and benefit future players. The enhanced transparency of the International Draft that we have proposed best addresses the root causes of corruption in the current system."Nov. 18, 2026: Manfred says no room for compromise on capSpeaking to the media at the owners meetings in New York, MLB commissioner Rob Manfred said while there's room for compromise in general with the MLBPA, there's no room for compromise on the proposed cap and floor on team payrolls. "The owners want a deal with a salary cap and floor," he said. "I can't imagine the owners ratifying a deal that does not include a cap and floor," Manfred also said. "... Thirty clubs are 100 percent unanimous in support of the proposals that have been made. I'm not in a position to speculate about what happens in the event that we don't achieve our overriding objective, which is to get a cap and floor system that addresses the competitive problem that our fans perceive."MLBPA interim head Bruce Meyer, who has insisted that the union will never accept a salary cap, pushed back again."There can be no clearer example of the league's lack of seriousness than their insistence that they will not negotiate over the economics outside of a radical change to the system that would dramatically reduce overall player compensation for all categories of players and strip fundamental rights from players like the ability to have truly guaranteed contracts," he said Wednesday in a statement. 
"There should be no illusions about the owners' true motivation in pushing for this system. They want to make more money in profits and franchise values by artificially suppressing player salaries."To date, the league has tied every individual proposal to the players' acceptance of a cap-and-floor system. The players through their union have historically shown no willingness to discuss a cap on payrolls. Nov. 17, 2026: MLBPA head says 'We've wasted months of time'MLB Players Association executive director Bruce Meyer said MLB is not serious about preventing the lockout and has "wasted months of time" trying to court public opinion when the two sides could have been having substantive negotiations.
"At the end of the day, this is going to come down to the bargaining table," Meyer told the Boston Globe. "And we have been for months, since May, looking for a serious partner in negotiations, and the league has insisted since May that they won't negotiate over anything economic outside of our agreement to a salary cap. In that respect, we've wasted months of time when we could have been having a serious negotiation. So I'd say the more the league is focused on things other than bargaining with us in good faith, I would say that's counterproductive."  Meyer also said the MLBPA has put forth proposals intended to promote competitive balance and correct the game's revenue disparity, but the owners are focused on a salary cap to "increase their profits and franchise values." He added that the two sides have made progress on non-economic matters, such as drug testing and gambling policies.Nov. 3, 2026: MLB proposes phase-in period for salary cap/floorTo allow for a "smoother transition" to a salary cap/floor system, MLB proposed delaying its implementation until 2028. That would give teams time to prepare and get their payrolls in order, and allow for a full offseason heading into the system. The current competitive balance tax and revenue sharing system would remain in place in 2027.
"We recognize that clubs will need a full offseason to prepare to operate within the cap and floor system. Therefore, with this offseason already underway, we proposed today to begin the cap and floor system in 2028," MLB spokesman Glen Caplin said in a statement. "This proposal would allow a smoother transition into the cap and floor system."MLB also upped its salary cap/floor proposal to $258.3 million and $180.2 million, respectively. Back in June, the league proposed a $245.3 million cap and $171.2 million floor. It says it is willing to discuss further phase-in scenarios for a salary cap/floor system.Oct. 8, 2026: MLB proposes 154-game season, postseason changesIn its latest proposal, MLB proposed reducing the regular season from 162 games to 154 games, and adding a standard off day to every week. The league also proposed extending the Division Series from a best-of-five to a best-of-seven, and allowing higher seeded teams to select their opponents in the Wild Card Series and Division Series. As with every MLB proposal to date, the 154-game schedule and changes to the postseason format are contingent on the MLBPA accepting a salary car/floor system.
Sept. 28, 2026: A 60-game mark could be crucial in 2027If labor strife lops off 60 or more games from the 2027 MLB season, then the consequences could be significant. The Athletic recently reported that if the forthcoming lockout extends into late May or so and costs at least 60 games, then most of the league's national broadcast and streaming contracts would be extended for another year, through 2029. That's significant because commissioner Rob Manfred hopes to bundle and centralize team streaming rights and share those revenues equally, and the current timeline would theoretically allow that to happen at the same time the national contracts are up for renegotiation. Tacking on another year to those national contracts would push back the significant windfall that owners and the league are expecting from that new media rights structure. As such, this is a heavy incentive, at least on the league side, to not let any labor stoppage drag into June. Sept. 2, 2026: Anonymous poll of players shows unity -- but not unanimity -- against capA poll of current MLB players across the full spectrum of salaries and service time conducted by ESPN showed strong resistance to the payroll cap and floor being demanded by ownership and league and being put forth as a precondition to every proposed change from that side. An excerpt: How open are you to a salary cap?NL starting pitcher entering arbitration: Not open.NL infielder making eight figures annually: Zero. No chance.NL infielder on two-year contract: Zero. Absolute zero.NL pre-arbitration journeyman: From what I've been told, I don't think it's good for the game. I just don't know if I know all the pros and cons of it. But, from everything we've been told, it doesn't sound like it's a good thing.NL reliever on multiyear contract: With the right criteria, I'd be open to it.AL starting pitcher in arbitration: I don't want it. In '94, they canceled the World Series, so if those guys can miss over half a year and miss the World Series, I think we're fully prepared to hold out for sure.AL catcher entering arbitration: I need more information, but perhaps I would listen on it.That's mostly strong sentiment that aligns with the MLBPA position on the cap, but it's not ironclad. MLB in negotiations and its public statements is seeking to tap into any existing divide between, broadly speaking, lower-salaried players with not much service time and more tenured veterans in their higher-earning years. There is a bit of a schism there, but it would take a substantial one to shift, in any exploitable way, the union's long-standing opposition to a cap-and-floor system. The ESPN piece covers an array of CBA topics. With the two questions related to the proposed cap, the responses can be broken down as 16 in mostly firm opposition to a cap and five not necessarily in favor but open to further discussions and reflection. 
Aug. 27, 2026: MLB proposes changes to roster rules, free agencyMLB proposed a series of changes to current roster rules that, in a statement, the league says are aimed at "creating more stability in rosters, getting the best players to the  Major Leagues more quickly, and accelerating the pace of the offseason." Among the rule changes included in MLB's proposal are:Weekly rosters that are set each Monday. Only roster changes necessitated by injury, bereavement, paternity leave, trades, and waivers would be allowed after weekly rosters are set.Teams would be allowed to carry 14 pitchers on their 26-man roster. The current limit is 13.The 10-day (position players) and 15-day (pitchers) injured lists would be reduced to one week and two weeks, respectively. The 60-day injured list would be replaced with a 12-week injured list.Yearly optional assignments to the minors would be reduced from five to four. Currently, players can be called up and sent down only five times per season. After that, waivers are required.Move Rule 5 Draft eligibility up one year and allow players selected in the Rule 5 Draft to go to the minors. Currently, players selected in the Rule 5 Draft must remain on the MLB roster all season.Two separate "Quiet Periods" at the start and end of the offseason that limit free agent signings between the first day of the Winter Meetings and Dec. 21. Trades would still be allowed throughout the entire offseason. In a statement, MLBPA interim head Bruce Meyer said an "artificial free agency window ... would reduce player leverage and create a game of musical chairs pitting player vs. player."All the proposed roster rule changes are contingent on the MLB Players Association agreeing to a salary cap-and-floor system.July 21, 2026: MLBPA proposes changes to draftDuring a negotiating session with the league, the players' union puts forth its own proposed changes to the MLB Draft -- changes that are, in essence, a rejoinder to the drastic overhaul earlier put forward by MLB. Among the changes the MLBPA proposes are: Continued draft eligibility for high school and junior college players and expanded eligibility in the college ranks to include sophomores;Preserving the current 20-round draft format;An increase in the amount of money allotted toward draft signing bonuses;Continuing to award additional competitive balance draft picks to small-market and lower-revenue clubs;Rejecting proposed hard slot bonuses and continuing to allow draftees to negotiate their bonuses;Allowing lower revenue clubs to increase their signing bonus pool for the draft and implementing automatic pool increases for lower-revenue teams that qualify for postseason play;A reduction to the penalties levied against teams that exceed their draft bonus pool;Allowing the trading of draft picks among teams, with some as yet unnamed restrictions;Moving the draft back to June.Additionally, the union proposes increasing the money payable to draftees under the incentive bonus plan and eliminating, according to the MLBPA, "the current practice of clubs deducting certain bonuses from players' continuing education benefits."The timing of the draft has actually been a concern for front offices for years, since it was shifted later in the calendar to coincide with the All-Star break in 2021. Holding the draft in July crams both that and the trade deadline into just a few weeks and making it more difficult to allocate resources.July 14, 2026: The sparring continuesCommissioner Rob Manfred and interim union head Bruce Meyer each hold press conferences on the day of the All-Star Game in Philadelphia. "I think that I have an ownership group that is more united than any group in my entire time of baseball," Manfred says, referring at least obliquely to the league's push for a salary cap. "They are a group that believes in what I am arguing for.""The supposed stewards of the game have spent an inordinate amount of time trying to convince those same fans that they don't have hope or they shouldn't have hope or that the product that they're paying to consume in record numbers is somehow broken," Meyer says of MLB's efforts to highlight perceived competitive-balance issues in the face of increasing attendance and television ratings. "I think it's perverse."July 1, 2026: Temporary roster size expansionThe MLBPA puts forth multiple proposals, many of them dealing with procedural matters for purposes of player health, safety, and wellness. They include: Expanding MLB active rosters from 26 to 28 (14 pitcher maximum) for the first 15 days of the regular season. Allowing for placement of players on the 60-day injured list as early as the November tender deadline.Reducing the number of permissible in-season optional assignments per player from five to three.Accelerating eligibility for the Rule 5 Draft and ensuring a Rule 5 Draft will be held in 2026 and each year of the next CBA.Providing MLB service time and salary protections to pitchers who are optioned to the minors over the All-Star break and or immediately after a game where they met certain performance thresholds.Enabling all players to access club-collected non-proprietary performance data and video.The union's latest proposal is a reminder of the breadth of CBA discussions. Most issues are not the big-ticket items like a salary cap or lack thereof or revenue sharing structure but instead are somewhat esoteric matters that strike most fans as mundane. To players and teams, though, they're important considerations and in some instances may even provide a foundation of common ground moving forward. June 25, 2026: Limited free-agency contractsMore face-to-face negotiations take place, and MLB proposes more changes to the free-agency system, among other asks. MLB's latest proposal includes the following, all of which depend upon the union's acceptance of a payroll cap:A maximum contract length of five years for players who switch teams and a maximum of 15% of the cap with 5% increases every year of the contract;A maximum contract length of six years -- and a max of 16% of the cap -- for players who remain with their original team under a new "Cornerstone Player" provision;Based on the league's proposed cap figure for 2027, the maximum contract for a player switching teams is $202 million over five years and $265 million over six years for a player remaining with the same team;An increase in the minimum salary from $780,000 to $1 million for players with at least two years of MLB service time;An increase in the minimum salary to $900,000 for players with less than two years of MLB service time with the opportunity for a $100,000 bonus from the pre-arbitration bonus pool (already established);The elimination of deferred contracts;Acceptance of the union's proposal to allow free agency after five years of MLB service time instead of six for players age 30 or older;Acceptance of the union's proposal to do away with the qualifying offer system for free agents.MLB in a prior proposal called for a cap on team payrolls of $245.3 million starting in 2027 and a payroll floor of $171.2 million. The league issues a statement that reads in full: "The biggest issue baseball fans want solved to strengthen the game is fixing the payroll disparity that leaves too many fans without hope of their team competing for a World Series title. Every other major U.S. sport has tackled this problem, and every year more small market teams in those leagues have a chance to win. The salary cap and floor proposal levels the playing field, allowing us greater flexibility to address longstanding player priorities while sharing baseball revenue with the players 50/50."Today, in addition to proposing the largest ever increase in the minimum salary, earned by over half of MLB players, we accepted two landmark changes to free agency that have been in place for 50 years. We agreed to both the MLBPA's proposal to provide earlier access to free agency, and their proposal to eliminate the qualifying offer system, a provision players view as a drag on free agency. We also proposed to eliminate deferred compensation and to create a new 'Cornerstone Player' provision similar to the NBA's 'Bird Rights' to give every team a fair shot at retaining their fans' favorite star players."We will continue working with the MLBPA during the bargaining process to improve the game for teams, players and fans."The MLBPA responds: "After making a series of proposals to reduce player compensation by billions of dollars, eliminate fundamental rights with a salary cap, and destroy the amateur entry process, Major League Baseball and team owners are now attempting to distract from the true impact their plan would have on baseball. These misleading offers are designed to look like 'improvements' but are of little or no value, given they are expressly conditioned on agreement to the league's cap system which eliminates the free market, and ensures gains for one player only come at the expense of another. "The league also introduced a litany of additional restrictions on player rights — limiting salaries, contract length, performance, award, and signing bonuses. While MLB claims to be acting in the interest of fans, their proposals thus far are entirely consistent with owners' long-held goals: suppressing player salaries and maximizing club profits. "Owners' attempts to pit players against players are nothing new, but they've failed in the past and will fail again now, because PA members remain unified. We are committed to achieving a fair deal that protects the rights of all players, promotes competition, and leaves our game better for future generations."Lacking from the league's latest proposal, at least on the public-facing side, is any revisiting of the recent changes to the draft and any mention of prior proposed changes to the league's revenue-sharing system. During these same face-to-face sessions, the MLBPA proposes a ban on prop bets placed on individual players, ESPN reports. The idea is to preempt harrassment of players by gamblers. The proposed ban would extend to bets placed on individual player performance prior to and during any MLB game. The MLBPA also requested that players be permitted to engage in paid endorsements and sponsorships with sportsbooks and prediction markets. June 18, 2026: MLB proposes sweeping draft changesMLB and the MLBPA meet for face-to-face negotiations, and owners propose sweeping changes to the draft and also push for an international draft. As for the MLB Draft, formally known as the First-Year Player Draft, MLB pushes for the following changes:A reduction from 20 rounds to 12 rounds;A $200 million hard bonus system in which players are paid according to their draft position with no room to negotiate (teams have not spent $200 million or less in the draft since 2010);High school players would no longer be eligible for the domestic amateur draft, and college players would be draft-eligible at age 20."Over the last several years, college baseball has undergone a remarkable transformation," MLB says in a statement. "Expanded scholarships, NIL opportunities, revenue sharing and significant investments in facilities and player development have made college baseball an increasingly important pathway that is producing major league-ready talent at an accelerated rate. Today's top programs provide players with resources, competition and national exposure that were unimaginable a decade ago. Our proposal is designed to build on that momentum to benefit the game at the college, minor-league and major-league levels. By creating a draft system centered around college-aged players and making most college players eligible one year earlier, more players will benefit from both a college education and an elite development environment while reaching professional baseball -- and ultimately the major leagues -- more quickly. We believe these changes will strengthen college baseball and deepen fans' connection to the next generation of major league stars. We look forward to working with the MLBPA throughout the bargaining process to modernize the domestic amateur system in a way that benefits players, clubs, and fans." As for the international draft, MLB proposed making players outside of the U.S., Puerto Rico, and Canada (who are already included in the standard draft) subject to a similar system. The international draft would, as with the proposed changes to the MLB Draft, come with a $200 million bonus cap. At present, international amateurs may sign with any team under the international free agent system, although teams do have hard budget caps each year.The MLBPA also issues a statement in response to MLB's proposals:Today, MLB made another set of proposals that are flat out bad for baseball, ones that would cripple the next generation of players and damage the future of our game. They would, among other things:Eliminate over a billion dollars in player compensation from the international and domestic system over the next five years, with a $400 million reduction from 2026 to 2027 alone.Destroy fundamental player rights and remove talent from our sport by barring high school and junior college players (anyone under age 20) from the domestic draft.Abolish an entire year of international signings by delaying the first draft until at least September of 2027 (and as late as March of 2028), denying young international players the ability to start their professional careers.Players remain committed to bargaining in good faith and leaving baseball better than they found it -- the league's proposals fall woefully short.June 5, 2026: Trump supports a capU.S. President Donald J. Trump publicly supports MLB's efforts to implement a salary cap. "If you don't have a salary cap, you don't have a sport, because they can't help themselves," Trump says. "Football has a salary cap. They should have done it a long time ago."It's shocking, frankly, that they didn't put a cap on many years ago," he said, possibly referencing the 1994-95 strike. "They had a chance to do a cap, but they blew it."June 3, 2026: Manfred talks luxury taxSpeaking to reporters following the owners' quarterly meetings, Manfred addresses the luxury-tax system he and the owners seek to replace with a cap. "We have tried mightily over several rounds of bargaining to use a competitive balance (luxury) tax to address competitive concerns," Manfred says. "And sometimes you've got to admit you failed."We made a proposal on one set of topics. At the outset of negotiations, I went and said myself, 'We're open to whatever ideas people have, but we need a realistic framework that addresses the fans' concerns about competitive balance.' You just can't ignore that financial penalties have not gotten it done for us."June 1, 2026: MLBPA says cap is 'institutionalized collusion'In a call with reporters, MLBPA interim executive director Bruce Meyer addresses the owners' proposals. "Using MLB's definition of revenue and player share as set forth in their proposal and their presentation to us, player share under their proposal would go down," Meyer says. "Player share for this season, 2026, is projected to be well over 50 percent, using, again MLB's definitions of revenues and what counts against player share."Had MLB's proposal been in place in 2026, players, we estimate, would lose over half a billion dollars."Meyer also refers to a salary cap as "a form of institutionalized collusion.""Our salary cap-and-floor proposal addresses our fans' concerns by leveling the playing field while sharing baseball revenue with the players 50-50 like the other leagues," MLB spokesperson Glen Caplin responded on behalf of the league. "Under our proposal, major-league players will receive more compensation in year one of the system than in 2026. We are ready to listen if the MLBPA wants to counter our proposal at the bargaining table."May 28, 2026: MLB's first proposalsMLB and the owners publicly announce their first formal CBA proposal. Chiefly, they propose: A salary cap, including benefits expenses, of $245.3 million for 2027;A salary floor, also including benefits expenses, of $171.2 million for 2027;A 50-50 revenue split between clubs and players;The centralization and equal sharing of all local revenues.Using competitive balance tax (CBT), or luxury tax, payrolls as a guide, since they include benefits expenses, nine teams at present would be above the proposed cap line, while 12 teams would be below the floor. However, as Craig Goldstein points out, the amount needed to get all these teams below or above the relevant payroll thresholds amounts to an $18.7 million loss in aggregate player salary overall. Another sticking point will be how league revenues are defined. Owners no doubt seek to carve out things like real estate developments surrounding ballparks and ownership stakes in regional sports. As well, MLB's working definition of league revenues includes many expense deductions. On another level, the fact that Manfred is able to persuade large-market, high-revenue clubs to agree to equal sharing of all local revenues is a notable development. However, such a concession by those large-market clubs may be contingent upon the implementation of a cap. Another sticking point is that the league proposes an escrow system, as is used in the NBA and the NHL. This would mean a percentage of player salaries is withheld. If revenues fall short of projections, some of that money in escrow goes back to the league. If revenues are higher than projected, that excess is shared with the players. The MLBPA opposes the escrow system on the grounds that it undermines the notion of guaranteed player salaries. May 27, 2026: MLBPA's first proposalsThe MLBPA makes an opening suite of proposals to the league, including:A "competitive integrity tax" levied against teams that don't spend a minimum amount on player payroll.An increase of the minimum salary from $780,000 to $1.5 million.An increase of the bottom Competitive Balance Tax (more commonly known as the luxury tax) threshold from $244 million to $300 million.Increased sharing of local-broadcast revenues among teams but less sharing of stadium game-day revenues (the latter to incentivize on-field success).Tens of millions in extra revenue sharing to go to low-revenue teams that make the postseason or have a winning record.Free agency after five or more years, rather than six, for players who are at least 30 years of age at the time.Expanded draft lottery. Penalties for teams that neglect to spend revenue-sharing payments on team payroll.Draft picks and other incentives for low-revenue clubs active in free agency. Elimination of the qualifying offer for outgoing free agents.Increased compensation for lower-revenue teams losing players to free agency."Today, the MLBPA (Major League Baseball Players Association) presented a comprehensive set of economic proposals designed to advance the rights and benefits of players at all levels," Meyer says in a statement released by the union. "Our goal is to preserve and improve baseball's market system, rewarding competition on and off the field. Additionally, the players' proposals provide increased revenue sharing initially guaranteeing every small market club a minimum of $240m in revenue every season. This enhanced revenue sharing includes added protections to ensure clubs prioritize winning over profiteering. Ultimately, our proposals are designed to build upon the incredible momentum and popularity of our sport world-wide.""We appreciate the union making a set of proposals and we look forward to continuing the bargaining process and working towards solving the competitive balance problem our fans are telling us needs to be addressed," Caplin says in a statement. "We understand their proposals are designed to benefit players. Unfortunately, they do not address and in fact exacerbate the competitive balance problem our fans are telling us we must address. The MLBPA's proposal would reduce the amount transferred to lower-revenue Clubs, weaken the Competitive Balance Tax, and lead to even more payroll disparity than exists today. For example, under the Union's proposal, the Dodgers would pay less in luxury tax payments, giving them an additional $70 million to spend on payroll."May 12, 2026: Negotiations beginNegotiations on a new CBA formally begin between teams and players. Among the key issues to be discussed will be the league's desire for a salary cap, drastic changes to the revenue sharing system, league expansion, possible further playoff expansion, and an international draft.Dec. 1, 2026The 2022-26 Basic Agreement is set to expire at 11:59 p.m. ET, at which point owners are expected to lock out the players in the absence of a new agreement.

title: Ranking NFL division races from first to worst: NFC North, NFC South entertaining for very different reasons - CBS Sports
description: Plus, one division race is already over, per our projections
body:
Plus, one division race is already over, per our projections
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 24, 2026
                            
                    at
    1:29 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            4 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The NFC East might be the best example of the NFL's unpredictable nature. Earlier this season, it made history by becoming the first division to go winless over a two-week span in which every team played both weeks. Yes, that included the infamous Commanders-Giants tie that featured a fumble and an all-time clock mismanagement on the final two drives.Then in Week 11, the division went 4-0 collectively, with the Eagles, Giants, and Commanders all springing upsets over AFC teams currently in the playoff field. A $10 NFC East parlay of the Eagles beating the Steelers, the Giants beating the Jaguars, the Commanders beating the Bengals and the Cowboys beating the Titans would have netted you a handsome $345.51.As Al Pacino, playing Michael Corleone in The Godfather Part III, said: "Just when I thought I was out, they pull me back in!"Ahead of a packed Thanksgiving week chock full of divisional matchups, we rank all eight division races, taking into account the quality of the teams involved, the quality of the races themselves and the potential for pandemonium.
1. NFC NorthThe standings:Lions (8-2, 2-0 vs. division)Bears (8-2, 0-2 vs. division)Vikings (7-3)Packers (6-4)CBS Sports forecasting and projections:Lions: 51% chance to win divisionBears: 25% chance to win divisionVikings: 23% chance to win divisionPackers: 2% chance to win divisionThe NFC North's main quest is potentially being the first team to place all four teams in the postseason. But the division race itself is a thriller, especially with Lions-Bears looming on Thanksgiving. Yes, Detroit looks like the clear NFC North favorite for now, but a Chicago win on Turkey Day would boost the Bears' chance to win the division to 45%. Regardless, this race projects to end in a thriller: In Week 18, the Lions play the Packers, and the Bears play the Vikings.2. AFC WestThe standings:Broncos (8-2, 3-1 vs. division, 4-0 in common games)Chiefs (8-2, 3-1 vs. division, 3-1 in common games)Raiders (4-7)Chargers (1-9)CBS Sports forecasting and projections:Broncos: 50% chance to win divisionChiefs: 50% chance to win divisionDoes it get much better than a 50/50 split? Technically, our projections give Denver a 50.1% chance and Kansas City a 49.9% chance, if you're into that level of detail. The two teams have already played both of their head-to-head matchups (they split). The Broncos do have, on paper, an easier schedule remaining, which certainly helps.3. NFC EastThe standings:Giants (6-3-1)Cowboys (5-6)Commanders (4-5-1)Eagles (3-7)CBS Sports forecasting and projections:Giants: 55% chance to win divisionCommanders: 31% chance to win divisionCowboys: 14% chance to win divisionEagles: 1% chance to win divisionAll of a sudden, this division race doesn't look fun-bad and might just be ... fun! The Giants and Cowboys have the eighth- and ninth-hardest remaining schedules, while the Commanders don't face a team with a winning record until Week 16. A finishing stretch featuring Giants at Cowboys in Week 17 followed by Cowboys at Commanders and Eagles at Giants in Week 18 could provide plenty of twists and turns.
4. NFC SouthThe standings:Panthers (5-5)Buccaneers (3-7, 1-0 vs. Falcons)Falcons (3-7, 0-1 vs. Buccaneers, 1-0 vs. Saints)Saints (3-7, 0-1 vs. Falcons)CBS Sports forecasting and projections:Panthers: 50% chance to win divisionBuccaneers: 37% chance to win divisionFalcons: 9% chance to win divisionSaints: 4% chance to win divisionLast year, the Buccaneers beat the Panthers in Week 18 to stay alive, only to lose the NFC South on a tiebreaker the next day when the Falcons beat the Saints. Could we see similar madness this year? Week 12 will go a long way: If Tampa Bay beats Carolina on Monday Night Football, its chance to win the division jumps to 53%, per our calculations.The NFC South: It might be bad, but it's certainly not boring!5. AFC NorthThe standings:Bengals (7-3)Browns (6-4, 2-1 vs. division)Steelers (6-4, 2-2 vs. division)Ravens: 4-7CBS Sports forecasting and projections:Bengals: 77% chance to win divisionBrowns: 12% chance to win divisionSteelers: 11% chance to win divisionEven with the bunched standings at the top, our projections see Cincinnati as a clear favorite. The Bengals have several games where they should be huge favorites: Saints, at Panthers, at Colts, Ravens. It's far from wrapped up, though, and two games vs. the Browns loom large.6. NFC WestThe standings:49ers: 9-1Seahawks: 6-4 (2-1 in division)Rams: 6-4 (1-2 in division)Cardinals: 3-8CBS Sports forecasting and projections:49ers: 91% chance to win divisionSeahawks: 7% chance to win divisionRams: 2% chance to win divisionThe 49ers look like the best team in the NFL, and with a three-game lead in the division, this one might not have much drama. If that changes, it must start this week, when the Seahawks visit San Francisco. A Seattle win would only knock the 49ers' NFC West title chances to 81%, but it'd be a start.
7. AFC SouthThe standings:Jaguars (7-3)Texans (4-6)Colts (3-8)Titans (1-9)CBS Sports forecasting and projections:Jaguars: 94% chance to win divisionTexans: 6% chance to win divisionNever say never, but it's hard to see this one getting competitive, even after the Texans won and the Jaguars lost in Week 11. Houston needs another upset loss or two by Jacksonville. If that happens, remember Houston holds the head-to-head tiebreaker. That could turn up the heat.8. AFC EastThe standings:Bills (9-1)Patriots (5-5)Jets (3-8)Dolphins (1-9)CBS Sports forecasting and projections:Bills: 100% chance to win divisionWith Drake Maye out until the final week or two at best, it would take something catastrophic (basically a Josh Allen injury) for this to be an actual race. And then, Tommy DeVito trying to chase down Kyle Allen would be more sad than fun.

title: Urban Meyer 'concerned' about state of Ohio State program ahead of showdown vs. Michigan - CBS Sports
description: The former Buckeyes coach offered a vote of confidence for Ryan Day, but says fans have the right to 'point finge
body:
The former Buckeyes coach offered a vote of confidence for Ryan Day, but says fans have the right to 'point fingers' after a disappointing season
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 24, 2026
                            
                    at
    1:57 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            2 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Urban Meyer never lost to Michigan during his time at Ohio State, so he knows a thing or two about getting his guys ready to play the biggest game of the Buckeyes' season.This year's Buckeyes, fresh off their fourth loss that all but ended College Football Playoff hopes, are reeling down the stretch with a backup quarterback, inconsistency on defense and an elite coach who's facing unexpected pressure after falling well short of preseason No. 1 expectations."Am I concerned? I am a little bit. You just feel this (thing) around Columbus, Ohio," Meyer said this week on The Triple Option. "Who's gonna get fired? Who's not gonna get fired? Who's gonna stay? Who's in the portal? I'm hopeful that you walk into Woody Hayes facility right now and there's nothing but six straight days of 'How do you beat this team?' Am I concerned a little bit? I am. Not with the head coach, not at all.Over the weekend, Meyer started his unofficial Michigan-Ohio State preview conversation during an event at the Fawcett Center on campus, "Scarlet & Gray Saturdays: The Ohio State Football Story," which included Jim Tressel and Archie Griffin.
"The roster's better -- Ohio State -- but the best unit performing right now is the Wolverine defense. And that concerns me a little bit," Meyer said Sunday. "They really hammered UCLA. You got to think, the other side of the ball for the Wolverines is terrible — they're last in the country. And so, to still have decent numbers — only one team has over 21 points on them all year, and that was Oregon — that's a legit defense."When the conversation shifted to Ryan Day's future, Meyer said "there's not a finer coach in the land", but said fans have a right to "point fingers" given their investment in the program.Another storyline in the finale is junior Jeremiah Smith, who's likely donning an Ohio State uniform for one final time before declaring for the 2027 NFL Draft. The Heisman frontrunner, Smith, has 86 catches for 1,482 yards and 17 touchdowns this season and, with one more reception, sets a career-best in every statistical category.
Meyer expects Ohio State, as a 10.5-point favorite as of Tuesday, to win a tight game."On offense, we got the best player in the country, maybe the best player to ever play college football -- that's how good Jeremiah is. But we also have a backup quarterback, and the offensive line is not playing great," Meyer said. "So, I think this is going to be a rock fight, a low-scoring game, and I think whoever punches the hardest is going to win the game."I expect it to be a 17-10, 17-14 game and I got the Buckeyes."Day is 2-4 against Michigan as Ohio State's coach and snapped a four-game skid with last year's win. The Buckeyes haven't beaten the Wolverines in Columbus since 2018.

title: MLB rumors: Corey Seager willing to waive his NTC, plus latest on Mets, Cubs, Blue Jays, Guardians, more - CBS Sports
description: Here are your offseason hot stove rumors on Tuesday, Nov. 24
body:
Here are your offseason hot stove rumors on Tuesday, Nov. 24
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 24, 2026
                            
                    at
    1:34 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            5 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The uncertain 2026-27 Major League Baseball offseason is fully underway. The ongoing CBA negotiations and the near certainty of an owner-implemented lockout on Dec. 2 loom over all, and it may indeed mean a flurry of trades and free agent signings leading up to that date. That was certainly the case leading up to the last lockout of 2021-22, and this time around we've already seen some leading examples. Just recently, for instance, the New York Mets landed the biggest fish in the pond by signing ace Tarik Skubal to a record contract. Not long after, the Chicago Cubs fortified their rotation with Trevor Rogers and their outfield with Teruaki Sato, and Freddy Peralta is headed to the Baltimore Orioles. More's surely to come before lockout day arrives. Thanks to that prospect of a hastened pace, offseason rumors are flowing. Speaking of which, we'll be here each day to round up what's out there. You can find Tuesday's supply just below. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Corey Seager willing to waive no-trade clause to join Phillies
The Philadelphia Phillies are open to moving Trea Turner off of shortstop given that he's now a pronounced defensive liability. Speaking of openness, veteran shortstop Corey Seager of the Texas Rangers is willing to waive his no-trade clause to join the Phillies and upgrade the position for them, NBC Sports Philadelphia reports.Now 32, Seager will always have health and durability concerns, but he remains a plus defensive shortstop who produces well at the plate by positional standards. Signed to a 10-year, $325 million deal prior to the 2022 season (just before the last lockout, in fact), Seager is owed another $155 million through the 2031 season. The Rangers are reportedly looking to shake things up. The Phillies, meantime, are trying to keep their contention window open. It's a fit both ways, at least in theory. Such a move would likely mean a move to the outfield for Turner, who himself has very little trade value thanks to his ongoing decline and big contract. 

                            
    
                                                
                    
    Blue Jays targeting pitching
The Toronto Blue Jays have thus far failed to make a big addition this offseason, but they still have targets on the board. The Jays, after missing out on Tarik Skubal, Freddy Peralta, and Trevor Rogers, have moved on to targets like right-hander Kaima Taira out of Japan and lefty Adrian Morejon, the Athletic reports. Taira, 27, ranked No. 2 on our list of notable international free agents this offseason. Here's part of that write-up: "Listed at 5-foot-8, Taira gets outlier extension down the mound (close to seven feet despite his height), which creates a low release window. Hitters rarely see the ball come from where Taira releases it. He's not a gimmick pitcher either. Taira sits mid-90s with his four-seam fastball and backs it up with a cutter, sinker, sweeper, slider, changeup, and splitter. The sweeper and slider are distinct pitches, as are the changeup and splitter. The Seibu Lions used Taira as a reliever in 2024 and 2025, then started him in 2026, and he handled the assignment well. The breaking balls are just OK, and the fact of the matter is that pitchers this height don't often hold up under a starter's workload. I would assume the team that signs Taira will give him a chance to start. In the long run, though, he might be a reliever, perhaps even a multi-inning setup man. Taira was officially posted on Nov. 1."Morejon, meanwhile, is particularly intriguing. He's young for a free agent at age 27, and he's coming off a dominant season in the San Diego Padres' bullpen. Thanks to his elite stuff and full repertoire, he's also a strong candidate to transition to the rotation moving forward, though there's reporting that he'd rather stay in the bullpen. That makes him a coveted presence on the market, and the Jays have the resources and willingness to land him. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Cubs may not be doneAs noted above, the Chicago Cubs have been energized on the market lately, but they still have work to do after losing so many contributors to free agency. On that front, the club may be eyeing the aforementioned Taira, who's making the leap from Japan, the Athletic reported before the latest flood of moves.While Taira's role in MLB is TBD, the Cubs still have vacancies in the rotation for 2027 and beyond. 

                            
    
                                                
                    
    Guardians land Bubic
The Cleveland Guardians have agreed to a free-agent contract with left-hander Kris Bubic, Sportsnet reports. The contract is for $17.5 million over one year, according to ESPN. Bubic, 29, made nine starts for the Kansas City Royals last season, and after the trade to the Los Angeles Dodgers, he was used out of the bullpen. Bubic has an outlier fastball thanks to its rise and his unusual release point, and he's an interesting "ceiling" candidate in the rotation. However, his substantial history of injuries may mean he's best used out of the bullpen. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Tigers add Kim
The Detroit Tigers have added infield depth by agreeing to terms with Ha-Seong Kim on a one-year, $5 million free agent contract, ESPN reports. Kim, 31, is coming off a rough partial season with the Atlanta Braves, but he has a more palatable OPS+ of 91 for his career. He's been a primary shortstop in recent years and also has significant time spent at second base and third base. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Twins still looking for help on the marketEven after achieving a reunion with veteran starting pitcher Sonny Gray, the Minnesota Twins are still looking to fortify their roster for a return to contention in 2027. The club still hopes to make one more significant addition this offseason and add another player who may not grab as many headlines, the Athletic reports. Atop the wishlist are a first baseman or a second baseman and another lefty reliever. 

                            
    
                                                
                    
    Mets may be eyeing more rotation additionsEven after the splash addition of Skubal, the Mets may not be done adding starting pitchers in the service of a rebound season in 2027. On that front, the Mets may be interested in adding a starting pitcher on a short-term deal for next season, the Athletic reports. That would likely limit them to the back half of the market, especially with so many bigger names reaching agreements.

title: Snyder's Soapbox: Until MLB owners open the books, there's no reason to listen to pleas of poverty - CBS Sports

MLB owners are making tons of money, even if they won't admit it while they push for a salary cap

        Welcome to Snyder's Soapbox! Here, I pontificate about matters related to Major League Baseball on a weekly basis. Some of the topics will be pressing matters, some might seem insignificant in the grand scheme of things, and most will be somewhere in between. The good thing about this website is that it's free, and you are allowed to click away. If you stay, you'll get smarter, though. That's a money-back guarantee. Let's get to it.The world of Major League Baseball -- which includes fans and media, too -- has something rather heavy hanging over its head this offseason. Obviously. We know all about that pesky CBA expiration on Dec. 1 and we know that the owners are all but certain to lock the players out that night while they push for a salary cap in the name of parity.People are going to take sides, and I make no apologies for being firmly on the players' side. They are the talent and why we watch the games. No one is buying owners' jerseys and sitting in the ballpark facing the suites.Another reason I'm not a huge fan, in general, of the owners is that I don't believe we're ever getting the full truth about how much money they make. The Braves are publicly traded and we can see a good breakdown of how they fared in 2025. The short version is that they are swimming in money. We could look at the two recently sold MLB teams for a hint, too. The Angels were sold for $4 billion; Arte Moreno bought the team for $184 million in 2003. The Padres were also sold recently for $3.9 billion. The San Diego media market size ranks ahead of only Kansas City, Cincinnati, Milwaukee and, eventually, Las Vegas among MLB cities. 
And, again, sometimes you'll have an owner say the quiet part out loud. Enter Orioles owner David Rubenstein:"A lot of my friends were buying teams, and I realized they're making money. They're making more money than I'm making in private equity," Rubenstein said last month at a forum with other pro sports owners at the Economic Club of Washington, D.C. " ... I couldn't figure out why it is that people who are fans are so obsessed with the success of their local team. They're not going to make any more money. They're not going to go to the Super Bowl and get a trophy out of it."  People who cape for the owners: this is what you are defending. Obviously every owner shouldn't be painted with the same brush. Some of them are legitimately fans. But I'd be willing to wager pretty heavily that a majority of the owners think like Rubenstein here and view the teams simply as vehicles to make as much money as possible. Do we even need to bother with the suggestion that we shouldn't care about our favorite teams since they don't make us money and we don't get pieces of metal trophies? Sports fandom can be one of the purest and most wholesome things about our society. It brings families and friends together. It gives us emotions we otherwise couldn't even possibly imagine feeling. And I'll say this, too: I've seen my favorite team win the World Series and the absolute last thing on my mind was, "man, I'd sure like a trophy for my own mantle." The memories can't be matched by anything material at all. I would take nothing of real, tangible substance over those memories.It's maddening that an owner can be so out of touch with the product that he purchased. Do please hone in on the money comment, though. That's a much bigger deal. We've heard owners of some smaller-market teams cry poor for years and even decades, and the response from the MLBPA every single time is a pretty simple one. I reached out to a source and heard it again: "If any team wants us to believe they are losing money, they can simply open their books." 
Yes. The Braves have to and we can see how much of a money machine they are in the 11th-ranked media market (counting the two-team cities twice). Again, there will be exceptions, but the owners generally just view their teams as virtual ATMs, the output of which would be even higher with artificially decreased payroll because of a salary cap. At least one of them doesn't even understand why we care as much as we do. I remain firmly and proudly Team MLBPA.

title: Sean McVay on Puka Nacua: 'Can't say for certain' what his Rams future will be amid pending free agency - CBS Sports
description: Nacua is set to hit free agency this offseason
body:
Nacua is set to hit free agency this offseason
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 24, 2026
                            
                    at
    11:52 am ET
                        
                •
            
            5 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Los Angeles Rams wide receiver Puka Nacua is likely out for the remainder of the season after undergoing surgery for an MCL injury he sustained on the final offensive snap of the team's Week 9 victory over the Washington Commanders. Nacua is also set to be a free agent this coming offseason now that his rookie deal is set to expire, and Rams head coach Sean McVay delivered a mixed message about Nacua's future with the team."Yeah, we have a lot of guys that are free agents," McVay told reporters earlier this week. "What I've tried to really do is focus on right here, right now. He's obviously a guy that is a very important piece for us for now and for the future, but there are a lot of guys that fall under that category."That makes it sound like Nacua will be back with the Rams, and there's not much to speculate about. But a later quote indicated there may not be as much certainty on that front, mostly because McVay said those words pretty much exactly."I can't say for certain anything," McVay said. "Here's what I'm not interested in: something being taken out of context because my focus and concentration are on a Friday practice, even though I know it's Monday. I am trying to see how well we can play as a team against an excellent opponent [the Green Bay Packers] on Wednesday night.
"When you go through the amount of free agents that we have, Puka is a huge part of the conversation that you love, but there are also guys that are part of his draft class. There are guys on our offensive line, there are some guys defensively — so there are a lot of guys that are up that, as of right now, would not be under contract. There are mechanics that we'd like to be able to try to figure out how to keep these really good players and people that we love, and certainly Puka is at the forefront of our mind."In addition to Nacua, the Rams have Kevin Dotson, Coleman Shelton, Steve Avila, Byron Young, Josh Wallace, Colby Parkinson, Davis Allen, Davante Adams, Omar Speights and Kobie Turner, among others, set to hit free agency this offseason. While the Rams' $75.2 million in projected cap space is the fifth-most in the league (according to Over the Cap), that's a lot of players. Many of the Rams' pending free agents are significant contributors. However, none of them is nearly as integral to the team's success as Nacua is.Nacua is the Rams' best offensive player. He is one of the best receivers in the league, and he's well on his way to being one of the best in recent memory if he can stay healthy. His 383 catches are the seventh-most all time through four seasons despite the fact that he's only played 3.5 years so far. His 4,906 receiving yards are the seventh-most as well. He's the all-time leader in receiving yards per game (96.2), and he's averged over 100 yards per game in each of the last two seasons. 
But he's also somewhat unreliable from a health perspective, as a regular visitor to the medical tent and someone who will have missed 17 of the team's 51 games over the last three seasons by the time this year is up. And he's had very public off-field issues over the last year or so that resulted in a three-game suspension for violating the league's personal conduct policy. The league reportedly did not know Nacua needed season-ending surgery when it suspended him and allowed him to serve the suspension during his stint on injured reserve.It wouldn't be surprising, then, if the Rams were at least somewhat hesitant to commit what it would take to secure a long-term contract. The best wide receivers in the league are making over $40 million per year. Jaxson Smith-Njigba averages $42.5 million per year on his extension. To lock Nacua in, it would likely take a deal that exceeds JSN's average annual value, given Nacua's track record. Meanwhile, the franchise tag is projected to be worth "only" $30.91 million next season, according to Over the Cap, so that may be an option for the Rams to explore instead. That would allow them to retain Nacua for at least next season, even if they don't reach a long-term agreement, while also letting them negotiate an extension and retain the ability to explore potential trade opportunities if they decide they don't want to commit to him long term. And it seems like him not being around long-term is at least a possibility in the ether. 
"Very uncertain, up in the air as it pertains to the future with the L.A. Rams because going into free agency he's got two different injuries, including a significant MCL injury that Sean McVay says will keep him out a few months," ESPN's Jeremy Fowler said this weekend. "Probably ends his tenure with the Rams — plus the three-game suspension for the off-field stuff this offseason, so it's just not the kind of way you want to go into free agency with momentum. On the field, he's the best free agent in 2027 of any player, so the Rams have got to sort that out."Fowler may have misspoken when he said the injury probably ends Nacua's tenure with the Rams. Based on the rest of the quote, it seems like he meant that the injury will end Nacua's season with the Rams. But the idea that his future is uncertain at all is obviously notable, given how important he is to the team. If Nacua isn't going to be on the team, then the Rams don't have much to build their offense around in the future, whenever the post-Matthew Stafford era begins. They wouldn't exactly be setting Ty Simpson up for success if they decided to go that route. Because Nacua is so good and so important to the Rams' offensive infrastructure, it seems likely they'll eventually come to an agreement on an extension. But the lack of certainty in that regard, both from McVay and in outside reporting, makes this situation one to watch.
